description_ru: Каждый год Луна удаляется от Земли примерно на 3,8 см. Откуда мы это знаем, почему так происходит и что это значит для приливов, продолжительности суток и затмений?
text:
The Moon is leaving us. It does so very slowly, at about the rate your fingernails grow, which is roughly 3.8 centimetres a year, but it does so with absolute consistency. We know the figure with remarkable precision because the Apollo astronauts, and two Soviet robotic missions, left mirrors on the lunar surface. Observatories on Earth fire pulses of laser light at these reflectors and time how long the beam takes to return. The round trip lasts a little over two and a half seconds, and by measuring it to a fraction of a billionth of a second, scientists can track the distance to the Moon to within a few millimetres.

The cause lies in the tides. The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the side of Earth nearest to it than on the far side, stretching the planet, and especially its oceans, into a slight oval. Contrary to popular belief, and to many school diagrams, there are two tidal bulges, not one: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. If Earth did not rotate, these bulges would sit exactly under and opposite the Moon, and nothing more would happen.

But Earth does rotate, once every twenty-four hours, much faster than the Moon orbits, which takes about twenty-seven days. Friction between the oceans and the sea floor, and flexing within the solid rock itself, drags the bulges slightly ahead of the line joining the two worlds. The bulge on the near side therefore pulls forwards on the Moon, tugging it along its orbit. Like a child pushed gently on a swing, the Moon gains energy and moves into a wider path. Meanwhile, the Moon's gravity tugs back on the bulge, acting as a faint brake on our planet's spin.

The scale of the energy involved is considerable: roughly three and a half terawatts of Earth's rotational energy is dissipated as heat by tidal friction, mostly in shallow seas, which is about equal to the average electrical power generated by every power station on the planet. The result is an exchange of angular momentum, a quantity that is conserved in the system as a whole. The Moon gains it and climbs away; Earth loses it and spins more slowly. The effect on the length of the day is tiny, about 1.7 milliseconds per century, but it accumulates. Evidence for it lies in remarkably old records. Ancient eclipse observations by Babylonian and Chinese astronomers, recorded on clay tablets and bone, do not quite match calculations that assume a constant rotation speed, and the discrepancy fits a gradually slowing Earth. Even more striking are fossils. Some coral from the Devonian period, around 400 million years ago, shows fine daily growth bands grouped into annual cycles, and the count suggests a year of about four hundred days, each only about twenty-two hours long.

If the Moon is receding today, it was closer in the past, and the prevailing theory of its origin places it very close indeed. About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body, often called Theia, is thought to have struck the young Earth. The debris from this collision coalesced into the Moon, initially at a distance of perhaps only a few Earth radii. Some biologists have even speculated that the vigorous tides of that era, which repeatedly flooded and drained coastal pools, may have helped to shape the early evolution of life, though this remains a hypothesis rather than a conclusion. Seen from the surface, the Moon would have filled a sky many times larger than it does now, and the tides would have been immense, sweeping across the landscape twice a day with a violence we would hardly recognise.

Some of this history is genuinely uncertain. The simple extrapolation of 3.8 centimetres per year backwards would put the Moon on Earth's surface well within the planet's age, so the rate cannot have been constant. Tidal friction depends on the shape of the ocean basins, which have changed continuously as continents drifted apart and collided. Geologists have found rhythmic layers of sediment, formed by ancient tides, that suggest the recession was slower at some periods and faster at others. Reconciling these records with the physics remains an active field of research.

What of the future? The Moon will continue to retreat, and its apparent size in our sky will shrink. In perhaps six hundred million years, it will appear too small to cover the Sun completely, and total solar eclipses, as we know them, will cease. Humans are, in cosmic terms, and entirely by luck, living in a very special era, in which the two bodies happen to look almost exactly the same size from Earth.

In principle, the process could continue until Earth's day and the Moon's month become equal, at which point the two bodies would face one another permanently, as Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, already do. But this would take tens of billions of years, far longer than the Sun will remain stable. Long before then, the Sun will swell into a red giant, and the question will be academic.

It is a sobering thought that something as constant as the Moon is quietly, patiently changing, and that the same process which shapes our tides has also lengthened our days. We tend to treat the heavens as a fixed backdrop, a stage on which the drama of life is performed. They are, in fact, a slow-motion machine, and we happen to be watching a very small moment of it.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: conˈsistency, extrapoˈlation, disˈcrepancy. Слоги перед ударением сокращайте.
Звонкий «ð» в the, that, within: язык между зубами и голос включён, не «з» и не «д».
На конце слова month, growth: кончик языка между зубами, глухо, без добавочного «с».

questions.question: How fast is the Moon moving away?
How do scientists measure the Moon's distance so precisely?
questions.answer: By timing laser pulses reflected from mirrors left on the Moon.

questions.question: Why does the Moon recede?
questions.answer: Tidal bulges ahead of the Moon pull it forward, transferring angular momentum from Earth.

questions.question: What will happen to solar eclipses in the far future?
questions.answer: The Moon will look too small to cover the Sun, so total eclipses will end.
